items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: I know what I hear when I write music for the players and their concepts like Duke Ellington did

ctx.x: Were you getting a sense of maybe later on some of that experience when you started composing went back to those days when you were playing with saxophone players and getting an idea of how to orchestrate and arrange. Did you ever have formal lessons in that?

No. You know I’m self taught at that. So you know I know what I hear when I write music for the players and their concepts like Duke Ellington did, he used to write for all the personalities in his orchestra you know. So he wrote that way so the composition would bring the most out of the player, you know, and that that would be a reciprocal exchange in the dialogue, the musical dialogue.

What about changing keys for a different situation, if you’re backing up a singer or even yourself. Did you start to get this idea that the song is the same in any key, you just have to think of the one and the six and the two and the five and so forth. Did that start to sort of gel in your head?

items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I used to listen to those records and be fascinated by the music... which had, you know, Duke Ellington... The Bitches Brew sessions... Big room, beautiful room. It was a great room because Monk had recorded in there and Count Basie, Duke Ellington.

ctx.x: Now, when your grandmother first took you to get piano lessons was that because you had expressed interest in taking piano lessons or was that just you, because that's how a lot of folks got into because that's what was done. But, had you started to already exhibit or express a passion for music?

Well, I liked playing the piano. I liked listening to music. My uncle Roy had a lot of jazz records, like the old 78s. He used to have a Victrola that you cranked up and I used to play all of these at an early age, 5, 6, 7. I used to listen to these Decca records, and the Okeh records, and Columbia records which had, you know, Duke Ellington, Billie Holliday, Count Basie, Slim Gaillard, Dusty Fletcher. So, I used to listen to those records and be fascinated by the music even before I knew it was jazz. I actually…
